resources.string: Chooses the DS renderer. Vulkan is the default and supports higher internal resolutions; Software renders at native 1x resolution and can resolve some graphics or driver problems. DS 2D rendering can still be CPU-heavy, so Vulkan is not faster in every game. Start with Vulkan; try Software for a specific compatibility problem and compare the same scene.

Raises the internal resolution of DS 3D graphics when using Vulkan. Higher values improve 3D edges but increase GPU load, memory use and heat; native 2D artwork gains little detail. Software always uses native 1x. Start at the default 2x and reduce to 1x if the game slows down; increase only when performance stays stable.

Chooses flat covers, 3D box artwork or no covers in the library. This changes library appearance and image downloads/cache use, not game graphics or emulation speed. Use the style you prefer; disable covers to avoid artwork loading and reduce library image storage.

Mirrors the selected replacement camera image horizontally, vertically or in both directions before a 3DS game sees it. This corrects its orientation, not camera quality or game speed. Start with None and flip only when the image appears reversed in the game.

Darkens the selected background so text and controls remain readable. Higher percentages hide more of the artwork; this does not change game brightness or rendering quality. Increase it until menu labels are easy to read and reduce it to show more artwork.

Chooses the colours and appearance of the app interface. System follows the device light/dark preference; other choices keep their own appearance. This does not change game graphics. Start with System or Dark, and choose another theme for comfort or better contrast.

Routes mapped keyboard buttons to the selected player port. Changing it affects which player receives input, not keyboard sensitivity or game speed. Use Player 1 for solo play and another supported port only when controlling an additional player.

Routes mapped mouse buttons and aim input to the selected player port. An unsupported port may receive no input in that console or game. Use Player 1 for solo play; select another supported port only for multiplayer.

Turns mouse-wheel movement into pulses on the selected emulated buttons or stick directions. This changes the wheel mapping, not camera sensitivity. Leave it Off unless you need a wheel shortcut; choose controls the current console and game actually use.

Sets how long each emulated input from a mouse-wheel step remains pressed. A longer pulse is easier for games to detect but can repeat or hold an action too long. Start at the default; increase if steps are missed and decrease if each step causes too much movement.

Scales mouse movement sent to the selected emulated stick. Higher values reach strong stick input with less mouse travel but make fine aiming harder; this does not raise the game frame rate. Start at 100% and adjust to the game and your mouse.

Scales vertical mouse aim relative to its normal strength. Higher values need less mouse travel to look up or down but can make vertical aiming less precise. Start at 100%; lower it if vertical motion feels too fast compared with horizontal motion.

Filters small changes in mouse aim to reduce jitter. Higher values can steady movement but add response delay and make quick turns feel less direct. Start low and increase only enough to remove distracting jitter.

Ignores small mouse-aim movements before they become emulated stick input. A larger deadzone can suppress drift or noise but also loses fine corrections. Start at the default and raise it only if the view moves when you intend to keep it still.

Exchanges the displayed positions of the two console screens. For DS, touch input follows the touchscreen to its new position; swapping does not change the guest game state or improve performance. Keep the normal order unless the other screen position is easier to see or reach.

Sets how much horizontal space the docked second-screen panel occupies. A wider panel makes that screen easier to read but leaves less room for the main screen. This changes the layout, not internal resolution. Start at the default and widen it only as needed.

Changes the emulated 3DS CPU clock relative to the real console. A higher value may reduce guest CPU slowdowns but requires more host CPU work; a lower value may improve host performance while causing guest slowdowns or timing problems. Keep 100% normally and change it only for a tested game-specific reason.

Selects New 3DS hardware instead of the original model, including its additional CPU resources and memory. Some games require New 3DS; changing the model can affect compatibility and workload. Keep New 3DS enabled unless a particular game needs the original model. Restart the game after changing it.

Sets the region reported by the emulated 3DS. Region can affect compatibility, available languages and regional game behaviour; it does not directly improve performance. Use Auto to match the game, and select a region manually only when the game requires it.

Sets the 3DS system language reported to games. Games may use it to select text or voices, but only languages included in that game are available. Choose your preferred supported language; use the game settings if it ignores the system language. This does not change app language or performance.

Bypasses the 3DS region check so a title from another region can start. It can help region compatibility but does not translate the game or increase speed. Leave it disabled when the game boots normally; enable it only when a region mismatch prevents launch.

Adjusts audio duration when emulation cannot maintain real-time speed, reducing gaps and crackling. It may alter the sound slightly and does not make the game itself faster. Keep it enabled for smoother audio; disable it only when testing a sound problem or when you prefer unmodified timing.

Adjusts audio scheduling using measured emulation speed instead of only the guest clock. This can change audio behaviour when speed fluctuates and may help some timing problems. Leave it disabled normally; enable it only if comparison in the same game confirms better sound.

Sets the emulated audio level before Android applies its own volume. Lower values make the game quieter without changing game speed or audio accuracy. Start at 100% and use device volume for normal listening; lower this value to balance a loud game against other audio.

Selects microphone input for the 3DS: Auto chooses an available input backend, None sends silence and Static Noise supplies generated noise. This affects games that listen for sound, not speaker volume or performance. Start with Auto; use noise for a blowing action or None when microphone input is unwanted.

Chooses the 3DS hardware graphics backend: Vulkan or OpenGL. Performance and correctness depend on the GPU driver and game. Start with Vulkan; try OpenGL if that game has graphical faults or unstable rendering. Restart the game after switching.

Uses more accurate multiplication in hardware shaders to reproduce certain 3DS effects correctly. It can fix graphics at some performance cost and only applies with hardware shaders. Leave it disabled unless it corrects visible errors in the current game.

Stores compiled shader data on disk for reuse on later runs. This can reduce repeated shader-compilation pauses but uses storage; it does not eliminate every first-time stutter. Keep it enabled normally and disable it only while diagnosing a shader-cache problem.

Synchronises presentation with the display to reduce visible tearing. It can affect frame pacing and input latency; it does not increase emulation speed. Keep it enabled for stable presentation and try disabling it only when comparing a specific latency or frame-pacing problem.

Skips presenting frames whose image has not changed. It can reduce graphics work and power use in static scenes, while the guest game continues running. Leave it disabled normally; enable it if it saves power without causing visible pacing issues in your game.

Raises the internal resolution used for 3DS graphics. Higher values sharpen 3D edges but increase GPU load, memory use and heat; they do not add detail to every 2D asset. Start at 2x if performance allows, or Native for the lowest cost, and raise it only while the game remains smooth.

Applies an upscaling filter to game textures. It may smooth or reshape pixel artwork and adds processing cost; the best-looking filter depends on the game. Start with None for original textures and best performance, then compare filters only if you prefer their appearance.

Chooses the arrangement and relative sizes of the two 3DS screens. A larger main screen improves readability while a hidden or smaller touchscreen may be harder to use. This changes presentation rather than internal rendering resolution. Start with both screens visible and choose a layout that fits the game.

Exchanges the roles of the two 3DS screens in the selected layout, including which screen is large or shown alone. It changes presentation and touchscreen placement, not game speed. Keep the normal order unless the game is easier to play with the other screen prominent.

Changes the shape used to display the 3DS image. A wider or stretched shape fills more of the device screen but can distort circles, text and characters; it does not add native image detail. Start with the normal aspect ratio and stretch only if you prefer the result.

Provides the emulated 3DS with an SD card stored in the emulator data folder. Games and homebrew can use it for extra data; disabling it can make that content unavailable. Keep it enabled unless diagnosing an SD-related problem, and back up data before changing storage settings.

Selects the source of emulated 3DS motion input: the app-provided emulation source or an external CemuHook UDP server. Choosing a source without input makes motion controls unresponsive and does not improve game speed. Use Emulated normally; choose UDP only after configuring a working server.

Selects whether 3DS touchscreen input comes from the emulation window or an external CemuHook UDP server. Choosing UDP without a configured source can stop normal touch control. Use Emulation Window for on-device play and UDP only for an intentional external-input setup.

Selects which of four controller slots supplies input from a CemuHook UDP server. A mismatched slot can leave remote input unresponsive; it does not change local controller assignment or performance. Start with Pad 1 and change it only to match the slot used by your server.
